title: Why the gopis envied a flute
hookLine: a gopi is jealous of a piece of bamboo, and the hollow reed turns out to be the lesson
carry: empty of ego, like krishna's flute
tomorrow: who answers when the flute calls at night?

lines: CLOSER TO HIM THAN ANY OF THEM.
FROM THE SIDE OF THE FLUTE.
cards: What did a stick do to deserve this? That's the gopis' question, and they're not joking. They're still in the village, still listening, and one of them says what the others are thinking.
Krishna's lips are on that flute all day. It's a length of bamboo cut from some riverbank, with no voice of its own, no family, no story. And it gets closer to him than any of them.
So they ask, half in envy and half in wonder: what good thing did this flute ever do?

teach.h: WHAT GOOD DID THIS FLUTE EVER DO?
teach.b: The Bhagavata gives the question to one gopi. What good did this flute ever do, she asks, that it enjoys the sweetness of his lips, a sweetness the gopis feel is theirs, and leaves them only what's left over?
Then she answers herself, in a strange and lovely way. She looks at the bamboo's family.

teach.h: THE RIVERS AND TREES ARE PROUD.
teach.b: The lakes and rivers whose water raised it are glad: their lotuses open like hair standing up on skin.

And the trees, the bamboo's elders, let their sap run down like tears, the way old people weep with joy when someone in the family turns out devoted. So halfway through her sentence, envy turns into praise.
Now look at what a flute is.

teach.h: A HOLLOW REED, NOTHING IN THE WAY.
EMPTY OF EGO, FULL OF HIS MUSIC.
teach.b: Breath goes in one end and comes out as music; the flute adds nothing but the empty space.
This is one of the best-loved readings in Krishna devotion: the flute is close to him because there's nothing inside it in the way. A reed packed full makes no sound.

So the devotee's prayer is to be hollowed out, emptied of ahankara, the ego that keeps saying me and mine, so that Krishna's breath makes the music. Devotees call him Murlidhar, the one who holds the flute.
That's a reading teachers give, not a line in the chapter. The chapter just leaves us with a woman in a village, jealous of a piece of bamboo, and then glad for it.

how: Devotees sing and recite the gopis' words about the flute from the Bhagavata, honor Krishna as Murlidhar, the one who holds the flute, and many close an action with Krishnarpanam astu, offering it to him.

o: a reed the gopis cut from the riverbank for him
the stick Krishna uses to drive the herd home
the hollow reed at Krishna's lips that the gopis envy

games.q: the gopi's question — tap the pairs.
p: nothing in the way of his breath

s: the gopis are simply happy for the flute
they start out envious: it gets the sweetness of his lips and leaves them what's left.
the bamboo's 'family' of rivers and trees rejoices
the lotuses open and the trees weep sap like proud elders.
the chapter says the flute stands for an empty heart
that's a reading some devotional teachers give; the chapter itself is the gopis talking.

games.q: at katha, an auntie says she prays to be 'krishna's flute.' by the gopis' chapter, what does she mean?
o: she wants to learn to play music for him.
she wants to be emptied of ego, so his breath plays through her.
she wants to be closest to him, ahead of everyone else.
games.why: a flute is hollow; it adds nothing but room. teachers read it as the devotee with the ego cleared out, so Krishna makes the music.

practice: Many Krishna devotees close a task or a meal with two words: Krishnarpanam astu, let this be an offering to Krishna. It hands the credit back, the way a flute hands back the breath.

Breathe like a reed now: in without grabbing, out without pushing. With each exhale, let go of one small need to be right, or noticed, or first. Then pick one thing you will do today and offer it ahead of time.
If you pray, say the words. If you don't, just picture doing it with nothing of yours in the way.

wordCard.voice: The flute. A hollow length of bamboo that the gopis envy, because it is always at Krishna's lips.

orig.note: Hindi, from Sanskrit: the flute. Devotees call Krishna Murlidhar, the one who holds the flute.

carryVoice: Your line: empty of ego, like Krishna's flute. Tomorrow: who answers when the flute calls at night? See you then.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.21, the gopis' question about the flute's good deeds and its rejoicing 'family' of rivers and trees
